context: factory · block machine and curing for concrete blocks, or dryer and kiln for clay bricks

brief.intro: New to this project type? There are two different factories behind this name. A concrete block plant batches a dry concrete, presses it into blocks or pavers in a vibrating machine, moves the fresh blocks on boards into curing chambers for a day, then cubes and wraps them — a compact, automated line. A clay brick plant prepares clay, extrudes and cuts it, dries the green bricks slowly in a dryer and fires them for days in a long tunnel kiln; the kiln and dryer are large refractory structures that take months to build and weeks to heat up. In both, the building is a simple shed. The schedule is set by the production line order, the foundations for the press or the kiln, and the long start-up — especially drying and heating the kiln.

scope.desc: Natural gas / fuel supply, Compressed air, Process water, Dust extraction — the services every machine needs before it can run.

glossary.plain: a press that vibrates and compacts dry concrete into blocks or pavers on a board.
a freshly formed brick or block that has not yet hardened or been fired.
a closed room where blocks harden in warm, damp air.
a long kiln through which cars loaded with bricks move slowly past the firing zone.
the heat-resistant wagon that carries bricks through the dryer and kiln.
heat-resistant brick or lining inside the kiln.
slowly heating new refractory to drive out moisture before full temperature; rushing it cracks the lining.
the machine that stacks finished blocks into cubes for strapping and dispatch.

must_get_right: Decide early which plant it is — concrete block or fired clay — because the clay plant adds a kiln and dryer that roughly double the installation and start-up time.
The kiln is built by specialist refractory masons to a strict sequence; it cannot be accelerated by adding labour once the casing is closed.
Gas supply and its approval are prerequisites for kiln dry-out; track the gas connection as a milestone.
Kiln dry-out and heat-up follow a fixed temperature curve over days or weeks — schedule it as a continuous, non-compressible activity.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities are organised by plant area along the process line and by discipline, with every long-lead machine tracked from order to factory test, shipping and arrival.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Standard site calendar for construction; equipment installation may run extended shifts under vendor supervision. Commissioning follows the vendor's programme, and hot commissioning runs continuously once started.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: Supplier drawings → machine, kiln and dryer foundations → building → line installation in parallel with kiln steel and refractory → gas, power and air → dry runs → kiln dry-out and heat-up → first products → quality tests. The critical path runs through the kiln (clay) or the production line delivery (blocks).

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: The process technology and vendor are fixed before design starts; vendor drawings for foundations arrive on the agreed dates; permanent power and water are available before cold commissioning; raw material for trial production is on site.

sections.heading: Procurement & long-lead items
sections.body: The schedule tracks the following as milestones because they drive the programme:

rows: Block machine / extrusion line with handling

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Heavy machines need crane access and often must enter before the cladding or a wall is closed. Vendor supervisors are booked for fixed periods. Clean, dry, powered conditions are required before precision equipment is unpacked.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Main risks: late production line, refractory work behind programme, late gas connection, cracked lining from a rushed dry-out, and product quality during start-up. Contingency is held before first saleable production.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3 by plant area and discipline; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the installation crews and the vendor supervisors — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
